item.content:encoded:
Mindful Intimacy: How mental health affects relationships
It starts with the ‘partner problem’. We’re taught from a young age that we must find a partner to live out our lives with. It shapes a deep, sometimes unshakeable desire for one person to be faithful to and intimate with. But what happens to intimacy with another when your internal experience of yourself keeps changing? It’s a dilemma rarely explored on screen. So when I saw that episode of Modern Lovess with Anne Hathaway, evidently living out scenes from my life and proclaiming, “I’m bipolar”, I knew someone understood me.
I was diagnosed with Bipolar II Disorder in late 2018. I’m obviously not alone—India’s National Mental Health Survey data from 2016 suggests that about 0.3-0.5 per cent of India’s population, suffers from Bipolar Affective Disorder (BPAD). I got a diagnosis and started treatment—a 2023 study found that there’s a 70.4 per cent treatment gap among people with current bipolar disorder in India. Honestly, receiving the diagnosis was a relief. I’d had years of prolonged depressive episodes on and off, but I couldn’t explain the manic, hyperactive and hyper-productive stints in between. The diagnosis, paired with a prescription and a treatment plan that included self-compassion, meant I could finally ‘be better’. In 2022, a psychiatrist diagnosed that I had attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) symptoms too. I read up on the incidence of bipolar disorder and ADHD occurring in people at the same time, and was surprised to find that it’s not uncommon at all—as of the 2020s, one in 13 adults with ADHD globally can be expected to experience bipolar disorder.
A diagnosis alone, however, doesn’t always lead to addressing challenges with one’s love life. I’ve had therapists and psychiatrists gloss over, even do an eye roll when I bring up romantic conflicts as major triggers. Some of the key conflicts any person with advanced mental health issues can struggle with, such as with self-image, body image, rejection dysphoria, loss of or excessive libido, are all deeply linked with the ability to find and maintain a romantic partnership. Dr Sneha Sharma, psychiatrist and founder of Anvaya Care in the Delhi-NCR region, tells me, “I can’t speak about other psychiatrists… but if [we] are not intentional about understanding the effects of treatment, medication and diagnosis [on interpersonal relationships] then overall wellbeing isn’t being taken into account...a patient might relapse [based on] on how a partner might perceive them, and those factors can precipitate an episode”. If not in the first sitting, the conversation on relationships needs to be intentionally brought forth by mental health practitioners, Dr Sharma insists.
A diagnosis can also sometimes lead to a stalling mechanism, even if inadvertently. Astha Ahluwalia, a Gurugram-based psychologist, says she finds that “for some, dating is postponed with a diagnosis: they think ‘I need to sort my mental health out first’. Sometimes that is genuinely what someone needs, but I wonder whether ‘working on myself’ can also become a safe space over allowing oneself to be vulnerable with another person. Sometimes diagnosis can also become a lens to assess almost every emotional reaction or relationship difficulty… something to hide behind, particularly when accountability and facing our own contribution to relational patterns feels harder”.
Then there’s the crucial challenge of sharing a diagnosis with a partner-in the-making. Ray (name changed), a friend from a BPAD support group in Delhi-NCR, has been adamant in his guidance to me: “Diagnosis is just that; it is not your identity. If you conflate identity and diagnosis, and lead with that, you shut doors to other opportunities.” His advice has always been not to disclose a diagnosis “the first couple of dates”. “Only when things progressed and when it was clear that I could trust the other person, would I share that I live with bipolar disorder. Sites like JeevanSaathi.com were a disastrous experience…the most people could relate to were words like ‘anxiety’ and ‘depression’—dropping the words ‘bipolar disorder’ was like dropping a bomb.”
Ray is now happily married, but he only shared his diagnosis with his wife after a few dates, and she had shared that she sought treatment for depression and was working with a therapist.
I myself have struggled with not sharing. A few months into my treatment, I tried dating during a hypomanic phase. I found myself matching with men who wanted to talk post 10PM, once they were away from the gaze of their prying parents. Treating mental health conditions require sleeping early—not entirely conducive for late night texting. My drowsiness would signal a lack of interest. In my hypomanic phases I’d either excessively crave nothing other than to work long hours, or nothing more than to explore my sexuality. I’d lock in. In both scenarios it would negatively affect my physical health, but also my prospects. When it was the former, I’d forget to eat, hydrate and occasionally medicate, and romantic partners’ appeals to talk or meet would be met with barefaced irritation, or just plain ghosting. In the latter scenario, I’d chase physical intimacy over genuine connections—it sometimes led to connecting with ‘one night stands’ who neither understood nor cared for protection, let alone aftercare. (A 2023 Indian study with a small sample size found that people experiencing acute bipolar depression reported high percentages of sexual dysfunction, up to 91 per cent. Mental health conditions are known to induce both sexual hyperactivity and sexual shutdown, depending on the phase of illness and treatment.)
The highs from both excessive work and excessive dating eventually led me to crash without warning. I’d ghost my paramours again, gladly. When I finally identified the pattern, I decided I would share my diagnosis in dating app bios, and let it serve as a filter. I can’t say whether this decision has paid off or not; Ray, and indeed a few other friends and relatives, have disagreed with this measure. I do know, however, that if I share my BPAD-linked limitations, and the ‘prospect’ cannot or will not understand, perhaps said prospect is not for me.
I’ve had the ‘Anne Hathaway in Modern Love’ days—accidentally having one good look at that face in the mirror is enough to stop all date prep and to sink to the floor for a cry. For many others, the start of the dating process is not the problem. Saket (name changed), who also struggles with BPAD and anxiety, feels “it’s about maintaining the connection”. “The challenges that accompany mental health conditions and treatment mean that I can’t always sustain interest in the process.” The excitement invariably dipping is often brought about by waning moods. It’s not that partners or romantic prospects universally fail to understand mental health blocks. “Most people want to be supportive partners, but they aren’t certain on how to offer support, without neglecting their own needs,” says Pratiksha Tewari, a psychotherapist and learning space specialist at the Hank Nunn Institute (HNI).
Pratiksha and HNI paired up with Sharma and her platform Anvaya Healthcare earlier in 2026 to run a six-part discussion circle, ‘Dil, Dimaag, Dialogue’, which aimed to create a discussion space for persons experiencing mental health conditions as well as their partners. (Disclosure: my own collective, Izaar, helped design and facilitate this series, and I had the opportunity to attend each of these sessions.) “It was surprising to find a mix of regular and new people joining each time, with new inputs to dissect, but there was one repeated, shared concern that stood out for me: participants being in the distressing position of explaining themselves repeatedly… ‘How do I cope? Is it my responsibility to explain, or should it be my partner’s to understand?’ ” Pratiksha says.
Pratiksha also finds that with increasing familiarity with therapy-speak, there’s an increasing use of certain terms or phrases as common parlance, which then find entry into relationship-making and placing responsibility on the other. “People struggle with navigating their relationships around the language of a mental health diagnosis,” she says. (For example, an ex-partner who repeatedly put his indiscretions down to his ADHD, making it tougher to ask for accountability) For Dr Sharma, the main takeaway from the sessions was how important it is to assess relationships during diagnosis: “As a doctor, I have underestimated at times the importance of relational experiences, and the impact it has on well-being, self-esteem, confidence, in relation to how others perceive us. To witness practically how much it affects people has been my biggest takeaway”.
It’s tough to negotiate mental health-speak, even when it’s supposed to induce a modicum of compassion or sympathy, and if possible empathy, in us. No doubt there are a few of us who have figured out how to insist on accountability, and stay genuinely accountable, while also being open with a mental health diagnosis. As for me, having hit perimenopause relatively early, I now find myself even more focused on managing myself over finding someone new. I am now increasingly leaving the dream of an ‘equal partner’ behind, in favour of quiet evenings spent alone or with understanding family and friends instead. It’s not that I’m completely closed off; it’s just that I’ve made peace with and make peace with the ambiguity of what the future holds for a 40-year-old menopausal BPAD woman in India. The more I’ve sought treatment, and the more I’ve conversed with friends, support group members and so on, the more I find I’m secure in not having an answer to the partner problem.

item.content:encoded:
British R&B star Liv East explores modern love on her debut album, ‘FUNKSOULSEX’
25 September 2026
Ahead of her biggest headline show to date at London’s Jazz Cafe on October 8th, British R&B star LIV EAST has released her debut album ‘FUNKSOULSEX’.
Laying groundwork with high-calibre production, intricate instrumentation, and raw, poetic lyricism, East moves fluidly across FUNKSOULSEX.
Exploring themes of seduction, lust, and longing, as well as female autonomy and the romanticised ideals of love, it’s a debut release that affirms her status as a thoughtful, dynamic, and potent voice in British music, navigating love in the 21st century and the blurred lines between desire and fantasy.
Speaking on the album, Liv East explains: “This moment feels like the perfect culmination of years of work, years of creating, years of slowly inching closer to myself sonically and artistically. I’ve always found myself slipping between genres, not out of not knowing myself, but out of never feeling the need to be anything other than what I am. So I decided to create my own genre: ‘FUNKSOULSEX.’ And whatever you feel when you read it, or hear it, is exactly what it is. The holy trinity of funk-infused, soulful, sensual music.”

item.content:encoded:
By Lee Minji
SEOUL, Sept. 22 (Yonhap) -- Korean auteur Lee Chang-dong is known for his grounded yet delicate portrayal of ordinary people, gradually unveiling them through the various layers that construct them rather than taking the easier way of labeling them.
The profound approach is epitomized in his Venice-winning masterpiece "Possible Love," his first feature in eight years since "Burning" (2018), which follows the lives of two married couples whose lives become intertwined in a way they had not imagined.
Their encounter takes place at a funeral for a laid-off worker who has taken his own life. The deceased is a former colleague of Ho-seok (Sul Kyung-gu), who had gone on strike against a mass layoff only to be brutally suppressed by police.
The traumatic experience still haunts Ho-seok, both mentally and physically, and as his wife Mi-ok (Jeon Do-yeon) gently reminds him not to drink alcohol, Ho-seok erupts into a fit of anger upon seeing documentary director Ye-ji (Cho Yeo-jeong) filming their conversation.
Meanwhile, as Mi-ok leaves the scene to get some fresh air, she runs into Ye-ji's husband, Sang-woo (Zo In-sung), as she searches for a loose wedding ring that escaped her finger. Unlike her brusque husband, Sang-woo appears tall, handsome and kind, as he moves his car to help her find the ring.
Following this encounter, Ye-ji is set on making Ho-seok the face of her documentary -- he has a sad face that only one person can have in the country, she tells Sang-woo -- and befriends Mi-ok, who seems more willing to speak on camera about the strike than her taciturn husband.
As their friendship deepens, Ye-ji and Sang-woo invite Mi-ok, Ho-seok and their young son Cheol to their fancy seaside home. Ho-seok, who first appears reluctant, eventually agrees to join them and even giving an interview on his experience.
But what seemed like a relaxed vacation at the picture-perfect estate -- which Mi-ok marvels at, describing it as a house that appears in a novel (to which Ho-seok responds: you don't read novels) -- sours in an unexpected direction as hidden desires and emotions surface.
At two hours and 44 minutes, "Possible Love" is not an easy watch. But Lee densely builds up the strength of the story in its nearly 3-hour run, weaving together unlikely themes, such as economic disparity, belonging and the moral boundary between a filmmaker and a subject.
The backbone of this process is the characters, whom Lee neither portrays in an obvious way nor turns them into subjects of mockery, while he does bring in moments of raw humor, such as when Mi-ok belts out an emotional trot song, to which Sang-woo plays the clarinet.
While Mi-ok is a working class mother who envies Ye-ji's luxury backpack and innocently raves about how much she adored Steve Jobs and how Sang-woo resembles him, she also has the dignity to tell Ye-ji that her stylish outfits are inappropriate for interacting with laid-off workers and their families. This side of Mi-ok comes to the fore in a symbolic seaside scene involving Sang-woo.
Sang-woo seems like a confident and compassionate person but the unseen hierarchy of power, deeply ingrained in his mind, is hinted by how he used to use a whistle as a child to call the family butler's son or how he tells Ye-ji she is "different" from the working-class couple.
In this film about filmmaking, Lee spends considerable time on depicting the agony of the laid-off workers who are called "the dead," in comparison with "the living," workers who managed to survive the layoff. He gives voices and faces to the laid-off workers in a counseling session scene where they take turns speaking on their emotions.
This part -- which Lee said he could not give up despite the risk of it making the film feel longer and duller -- perhaps serves as an answer to the underlying question of how filmmakers should treat the subjects of their films and whether their attempt to "love" them is possible or not.
Following a flurry of events, Mi-ok and Ho-seok return to their small home. Mi-ok complains that their home smells of trash but Ho-seok gently comforts her, saying that a little fresh air will clear the smell.
The film ends with a plainly elegant scene in which the couple sit in the moonlight, as they had as courting lovers, and share soju, leaving viewers a lingering trail of questions on the magnitude of money and class, but also a glimmering sense of relief on the possibility of love.
"Possible Love" is set for release Wednesday. It will be available on Netflix from Nov. 6.
mlee@yna.co.kr
(END)

item.content:encoded:
Love, they say, has many faces. Cruel, kind, manipulative; lately, though, love is artificial. As more and more people turn to chatbots for love or companionship, it does make one wonder: Is modern dating still a thing?
With the dating app fatigue at an all-time high, lovers and despos worldwide are starting to question whether it is all really worth it. Online dating is a trial by fire, but going on dates has progressively started to feel like entering the frying pan.
Perhaps that is where this swipe stress has come from. We know the result: a charred residue of any chemistry.
The premise of dating apps is enticing; it’s what draws you in: meet the love of your life (or the night) from the comfort of your couch.
But after the hundredth “So what brings you here” message, you start to wonder: Is that it? The urge to swipe becomes more powerful than the promised reward. It’s doomscrolling for love.
So while there may be a lot of fish in the sea. Being on a dating app is like fishing in the Great Pacific Garbage Dump. Useless and disappointing.
A 2017 study from the University of Bath found that an average UK adult has one in 562 chances of finding love on any given day. I don’t have the math to back me up, but trust me, a decade later that figure stands at one in a thousand.
Also Read: Where is my romcom moment? Hollywood promised it would happen at 27
RIP dating apps
If you found the right person for you in the middle of this geopolitical shitstorm, you’re one of the lucky ones. Also, the exception, not the rule. Modern dating is death by a thousand cuts.
Nothing is ever as it seems online. AI images are a menace (Google even made an ad about catfishing through it). And everyone is either a blogger or some type of “maxxer”; worse still, they turn out to be a manosphere junkie. Please take your red pill and leave; this is a safe space.
But in the midst of all that is also an emerging belief: I am better off by myself. Women, especially, are choosing not to be pulled back into a vicious circle of toxic relationships, putting someone else’s needs before their own and having to answer and adhere to all of society’s expectations. The male loneliness epidemic is not a result of women saying “no”, but of them saying “not anymore.”
In fact, a recent Institute for Family Studies survey found that the number of single young men in the US has increased by almost 50 per cent since the 2000s. And honestly, nothing threatens civilisation more than a million lonely guys with bad Wi-Fi and too much free time.
But in the face of plenty, of course, we will reject the available. After all, what if the next batch of matches is even better? Some apps are trying to find a solution to this. The League only shows you a select number of profiles every day. Hinge only offers eight free likes per day. And unless you message your match within 24 hours on Bumble, be prepared to lose them forever.
The crack in the shiny armour of modern dating is clearer than ever. And uncertainty rules the dating apps. It’s the ultimate will they or won’t they?
They say, “modern love is a cruel endeavour,” and to that I say, no s**t, Sherlock.
Views are personal.
